clinicalPearls: The core features are bradycardia and hypotension from reduced cardiac chronotropy and inotropy
Hypoglycaemia can occur, especially in children, in contrast to the hyperglycaemia typical of calcium-channel-blocker poisoning
Lipophilic agents such as propranolol can cause seizures, coma and sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening
Agents with membrane-stabilising activity or mixed effects produce more severe cardiotoxicity
Treatment escalates from fluids and atropine to glucagon, high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy and vasopressors
Refractory shock may prompt consideration of lipid emulsion or mechanical circulatory support
reference.pathophysiology: Beta-blocker overdose produces excessive antagonism of beta-adrenergic receptors, reducing heart rate and myocardial contractility and blunting the compensatory sympathetic response to hypotension. Impaired cyclic AMP generation reduces intracellular calcium available for contraction. Lipophilic and membrane-stabilising agents add central nervous system toxicity and sodium-channel blockade, worsening conduction and precipitating seizures. The net effect is cardiogenic shock with, in some cases, metabolic and neurological complications.
additionalDifferentials: Clonidine or other central sympatholytic overdose
Primary cardiac conduction disease or myocardial infarction
additionalInvestigations: Continuous cardiac monitoring and serial electrocardiograms
Blood glucose (may be low) and electrolytes
Assessment of the specific agent, formulation and co-ingestants
Blood gas and lactate to gauge perfusion
Echocardiography in refractory shock to guide support
redFlags: Profound bradycardia or high-grade heart block
Wide QRS or seizures suggesting membrane-stabilising toxicity
Ingestion of a modified-release preparation with delayed deterioration
reference.prognosis: Many patients recover with aggressive supportive care, but massive ingestions, membrane-stabilising agents and delayed presentation can cause fatal refractory shock.
pitfalls: Confusing it with calcium-channel-blocker poisoning (glucose typically low versus high)
Underdosing high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy in refractory shock
Missing delayed toxicity from modified-release formulations
